sections.title: Core Definitions & Pathophysiology
content: Bronchial Asthma: An inflammatory condition of the airways characterized by reversible airway obstruction, often associated with a history of atopy (eczema, hay fever).
Asthma Mechanism: Typically a Type 1 IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction.
Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD): A chronic, usually progressive respiratory disorder often triggered by viral or bacterial infections, particularly in winter.
COPD Mechanism: Often associated with long-term smoking and permanent structural changes; characterized by hyperinflation and reliance on 'hypoxic drive' in advanced stages.

sections.title: Immediate Triage: The ABC Screen
content: Step 1: Airway - Secure patency; check for stridor (upper airway obstruction).
Step 2: Breathing - Assess rate (RR >25 in severe asthma), cyanosis, and use of accessory muscles. Provide 100% Oxygen unless COPD CO2 retention is suspected.
Step 3: Circulation - Establish IV access; monitor heart rate and blood pressure.

branches: History: Atopy, family history, childhood onset, triggers (pollen/pets), smoking pack-years, winter exacerbations.
Examination: Bilateral wheeze vs. Silent Chest, Pulsus paradoxus (Asthma), Flapping tremor/Bounding pulse (COPD).
Investigations: Bedside PEFR, Laboratory ABG (pH, PaO2, PaCO2), Imaging (CXR for pneumothorax/pneumonia).

rows: Smoking history, chronic cough, elderly age.
Low PaO2, Low PaCO2 (High PaCO2 is ominous).
Low PaO2, High PaCO2 (Type II failure common).

sections.title: Emergency 'Silent Chest' Red Flag
content: Diagnosis: Life-threatening Acute Asthma.
Significance: Indicates so little air movement that a wheeze cannot even be produced.
Action: Requires immediate resuscitation; medical emergency.
Ominous Sign: A rising PaCO2 on ABG in a severe asthmatic signifies exhaustion and need for urgent intubation.

content.explanation: COPD patients may rely on hypoxic drive. High O2 (100%) can reduce RR, causing hypercapnia and coma. Start with 24–28% O2; check ABG after 30 mins.

sections.title: Signs of CO2 Retention (Asterixis)
content: Bounding pulse.
Flapping tremor (asterixis).
Warm, pink palms.
Headache and drowsiness.
Ocular finding: Papilloedema.

sections.title: The Ocular Beta-Blocker Contraindication
content: CRITICAL QUESTION: Always ask for history of Asthma or COPD before prescribing Timolol.
THREAT: Topical beta-blockers can cause fatal bronchospasm.
ALTERNATIVE: Betaxolol (cardioselective) is safer but still requires caution.

sections.title: ABG Interpretation: Simple Rules
content: Example Case: pH 7.05, CO2 2.0 kPa, HCO3 8.0 mmol/L.
Step 1: Check pH (< 7.35 = Acidosis).
Step 2: Check CO2 direction (Low CO2 is opposite pH; signifies compensation).
Step 3: Check HCO3 direction (Low HCO3 follows pH; cause is Metabolic).
Result: Metabolic Acidosis.

sections.title: Clinical Scenario: The Ophthalmic Ward
content: Choking: 5y/o with peanut/stridor. Action: Call help, ABCs, Heimlich maneuver (>1yr). Rule out anaphylaxis (rash/hypotension).
Post-Op Breathless: 75y/o 5 days post-vitrectomy, normal CXR. Diagnosis: Pulmonary Embolism (PE). Investigate: D-Dimer, CTPA.
Clinical Pearl: Severe breathlessness with normal breath sounds is highly suggestive of PE.

sections.title: Steroid Complications & Grading
content: Osteoporosis: Elderly asthmatic on chronic Prednisolone with back pain. Diagnosis: Vertebral fracture. Investigation: DXA scan (T-score < -2.5 diagnostic).
Steroid-Induced Glaucoma: Patient on COPD inhalers with IOP 34 mmHg. Mechanism: Steroids increase resistance in the trabecular meshwork.
PEFR Grading: Severe Asthma (<50% predicted); Life-threatening (<33% predicted). Diurnal variability >25% = poor control.
AKC vs VKC: VKC (Seasonal/Children/Spring); AKC (Year-round/Adulthood/Atopic dermatitis).

rows: Hydrocortisone 100mg IV (or 30mg Pred PO); IV Aminophylline 5mg/kg loading (20 min).
Hydrocortisone 200mg IV; Prednisolone 30–40mg PO; Antibiotics if purulent/fever.

sections.title: OSCE/Viva Picks: Cardiac & CPR
content: Cor Pulmonale: Right heart failure due to lung disease (COPD). Signs: Raised JVP, peripheral edema, loud P2.
Pleuritic Pain (Pneumonia/PE): Sharp, worse on coughing/breathing.
Ischaemic Pain (MI): Crushing, heavy, radiating to jaw/left arm.
Cardiac Arrest: 1. Shout for help/Call team. 2. Open airway (head tilt/chin lift). 3. Start compressions (30:2 ratio).

sections.title: Pearls, Pitfalls, & Highlights
content: Metabolic Memory: Long-term diabetes control benefits remain. COPD ‘metabolic CO2 retention’ means drowsiness without hypoxia.
Pitfall: Do not sedate an acute asthmatic; it suppresses respiratory drive.
Pitfall: Be as precise with 24% O2 as you are with 2.5% vs 10% Phenylephrine.
What not to miss: Always check for DVT in breathless post-operative patients.
Threat: General anesthesia in respiratory disease can cause 'ventilatory weaning' failure.

Scenario 1: The "Silent Chest" Red Flag
Question: A patient in the emergency department has severe respiratory distress but no wheeze is heard on auscultation. Diagnosis?. Answer:
Diagnosis: Life-threatening Acute Asthma.
Term: "Silent Chest."
Significance: This indicates so little air movement that a wheeze cannot be produced; it is a medical emergency requiring immediate resuscitation.
Scenario 2: The "Hypoxic Drive" Pitfall
Question: Why must you be cautious when giving 100% Oxygen to a patient with a long history of COPD?. Answer:
Pathophysiology: Some COPD patients rely on their "hypoxic drive" to breathe.

Scenario 6: Managing Choking in the Clinic
Question: A 5-year-old child swallows a peanut in your waiting room and develops stridor. First action?. Answer:
Immediate Action: Call for help; assess airway (ABC).
Maneuver: Perform the Heimlich maneuver (abdominal thrusts for children >1 year).
Differential: Rule out anaphylactic shock if there is a rash or hypotension.
Scenario 7: The Post-Operative Breathless Patient
Question: A 75-year-old patient 5 days post-vitrectomy becomes suddenly breathless. CXR is normal. Diagnosis?. Answer:
Diagnosis: Pulmonary Embolism (PE).
Clinical Pearl: Severe breathlessness with normal breath sounds is highly suggestive of PE.
Investigations: D-Dimer and CTPA.
Scenario 8: Complications of Long-Term Steroids
Question: An elderly asthmatic on chronic prednisolone complains of back pain. What do you suspect?. Answer:
Diagnosis: Osteoporosis and possible vertebral fracture.
Investigation Pick: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) bone scan (T-score < -2.5 is diagnostic).
Prevention: Use the minimum effective dose; consider calcium and vitamin D supplements.
Scenario 9: Steroid-Induced Glaucoma
Question: A patient on inhalers for COPD presents with an IOP of 34 mmHg. Connection?. Answer:
Hazard: Extended use of inhaled or systemic corticosteroids is a major risk factor for increased IOP and steroid-induced glaucoma.
Pathophysiology: Steroids increase resistance in the trabecular meshwork.
Scenario 10: Atopic Keratoconjunctivitis (AKC) vs. VKC
Question: How does AKC differ from VKC in terms of timing and age?. Answer:
VKC: Seasonal (spring/summer), typically affects children/young males.
AKC: Year-round (perennial), typically begins in late teens/adulthood and is associated with atopic dermatitis.
Scenario 11: PEFR Measurement Utility
Question: How do you use the Peak Expiratory Flow Rate (PEFR) to grade asthma severity?. Answer:
Severe: PEFR < 50% of predicted.
Life-threatening: PEFR < 33% of predicted.
Monitoring: Diurnal variability > 25% suggests poor control.
Scenario 12: Use of IV Aminophylline
Question: If a severe asthmatic fails to respond to nebulizers and IV steroids, what medication can be added?. Answer:
Medication: IV Aminophylline.
Dose: 5 mg/kg loading dose over 20 minutes.
Precautions: Adjust dose in liver failure, cardiac failure, or smokers.
Scenario 13: Heart Signs in COPD (Viva Pick)
Question: What cardiac findings might you find in a patient with chronic COPD?. Answer:
Term: Cor Pulmonale (right heart failure due to lung disease).
Signs: Raised JVP, peripheral edema, loud P2 heart sound.
Scenario 14: Differentiating Pleuritic vs. Cardiac Pain
Question: A patient has chest pain. How does the character of pain help differentiate Pneumonia from MI?. Answer:
Pneumonia/PE: Pleuritic pain (sharp, worse on coughing/breathing).
MI: Ischaemic pain (crushing, heavy, radiating to the jaw or left arm).
Scenario 15: The "Chain of Survival" in the Ward
Question: You find a breathless patient has collapsed and has no carotid pulse. First three steps?. Answer:
Shout for help and call the cardiac arrest team.
Open the airway (head tilt/chin lift).
Start chest compressions (30:2 ratio).
